A.explanation: About a factor of 10 too small, consistent with a power-of-ten slip in converting the 1 mm extension or 0.5 cm diameter to metres.

B.explanation: About a factor of 5 too small, consistent with using the 0.5 cm diameter as the radius so the area $A = \pi r^2$ is about 4 times too large.

C.explanation: Gives $E \approx 2 \times 10^{11} \text{N m}^{-2}$ from $E = FL/(Ax)$ with half the weight on each cable.

D.explanation: About twice too large, consistent with putting the full $80 \text{ kg}$ weight on one cable and ignoring that two cables share the load.

hints: Notice the wording two steel cables and the 80 kg man, so the extra tensile force in each cable is only half of $mg$.
Recall $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain} = FL/(Ax)$, where $L = 10 \text{ m}$, $x = 1 \text{ mm}$ and $A$ must be found from diameter $0.5 \text{ cm}$ using $r = d/2$.

Convert diameter to radius in metres, calculate one cable area $A = \pi r^2$, then evaluate $F \approx 400 \text{ N}$ per cable and compare stress $\approx 2 \times 10^7 \text{ Pa}$ with strain $10^{-4}$.
walkthrough: The extra weight is $W = mg \approx 80 \times 10 = 800 \text{ N}$. Because two cables support the lift, each cable carries $F \approx 400 \text{ N}$.
For one cable, diameter $d = 0.5 \text{ cm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, so radius $r = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ and area $A = \pi r^2 \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^2$.
Stress in each cable is $\text{stress} = F/A \approx 400/(2.0 \times 10^{-5}) \approx 2.0 \times 10^7 \text{ N m}^{-2}$.
Strain is $\text{strain} = x/L = (1 \times 10^{-3})/(10) = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$, with no unit.
Young modulus is $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain} \approx (2.0 \times 10^7)/(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) \approx 2 \times 10^{11} \text{ N m}^{-2}$. This is option C.
